title: Why columns buckle
summary: Euler's load and the length squared, end conditions, short columns that yield and long ones that buckle, imperfections, and the elastica.

steps.title: Euler's load and the length squared
steps.text:
A 3 m steel tube, 60 mm across with a 4 mm wall, pinned at both ends. Euler found the load at which a straight column can bend sideways: P_cr = π² E I / L². Solve it and read P_cr in the Summary (about 61 kN).

Now double the length to 6 m and solve again. The load falls with the length squared.

check.success: 15.2 kN: twice as long, a quarter of the load. Length is the enemy of a column.

steps.title: End conditions
steps.text: Back to 3 m. Fix both ends instead of pinning them. A fixed end stops the column turning, so it has to bend into a shorter wave: the buckled shape between its inflection points is only half as long (K = 0.5). The End conditions tab shows all four cases.

check.success: 243 kN, four times the pinned column. A flagpole (fixed–free, K = 2) gets a quarter of the pinned column's: 15.2 kN.

steps.title: Short columns yield, long ones buckle
steps.text: A 100 mm square timber post, 3 m tall and fixed at both ends. Its Euler load is about 400 kN, but the wood crushes at A σy = 210 kN first. Which one governs depends on the slenderness K L / r against π √(E/σy). Solve it and look at the Column curve.

check.success: Slenderness 52, below the limit of 72: a stocky column fails by crushing, not buckling.

steps.title: Imperfections
steps.text: No real column is straight. A bow of 5 mm grows as e0 / (1 − P/P_cr): at 95 % of P_cr it is twenty times larger, and the bending stress it adds yields the steel well before P_cr. The Southwell plot turns such measured deflections into P_cr: Δ/P against Δ is a straight line of slope 1/P_cr.

check.success: Twenty times the bow, and 2.8 times the yield stress. The first-yield load (Stress check) is what a designer uses, not P_cr.

steps.title: The elastica: a buckled column still carries load
steps.text: Small-deflection theory says nothing past P_cr. Euler's elastica, θ'' + (P/EI) sin θ = 0, follows the perfect column as it bends far: the load keeps rising, slowly. At twice P_cr a pinned rod folds into a loop with its ends turned through about 125°.

check.success: P/P_cr = (2 K(k)/π)² with k = sin(α/2). Real metal would yield long before: try it with a plastic ruler.
